doc.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023

title: From recording musician to road musician
summary: Scheduling around James Taylor and the Blues Brothers, the shift in his career, and the busy New York studio scene with Romeo Penque and Phil Bodner.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Yeah, I love that — “What’s your calendar like?” “Well I have to look.” And I was wondering when you go, this tour you’re on is fairly long, isn’t it?
When you get a call, when you got the call to do it, did you have to look ahead into your calendar and see do I have to bail?

Only like James takes priority, and we know that usually we’re going to be playing in the beginning of the summer. And so I just sort of make sure that I have open space you know. But also, the business has changed so much now. You know for instance doing clinics. I did a bunch of them this year but they usually want you to commit so far in advance that it’s difficult to commit to doing a clinic in March when you know that there’s a likelihood that the Blues Brothers Band is liable to go to Japan. And so I try to either have a codicil that if I have to bail I’ll get them somebody great — you know or else there’s been times with James where I’ve had to take time off and send in a sub to cover for me in order to do something that I was committed to and I had signed a contract to do. But you know I used to be a recording musician who went on the road. And now I’m a road musician who occasionally records you know. And that’s a natural progression you know they used to say like “Who’s Lou Marini?” “Get me Lou Marini.” “Get me a Lou Marini type.” “Who’s Lou Marini?” That was our path through the recording industry. And it makes sense because the business changes, new young guys come in, new young guys know their new young guys and that’s who they hire. So we talk about this. And when I first got to New York I was already an experienced recording musician from my years in Dallas because there was a very busy studio scene there with a lot of great world-class players. And so I was prepared for the New York studio scene. But guys like Romeo Penque and Phil Bodner who were on those classic Gil Evans albums

with Miles were my colleagues. I overlapped them in the studios. And they were very welcoming and mentors really with advice. So through the 70s and the first half of the 80s we had a busy studio scene going. Then the computers and drum machines and synthesizers began to eke — cut into our business and things, and you went from having ten big companies that did most of the music to a thousand in-house one-man guys who hired the guy that he knew from the University of Alabama to play on his jingle. You know that’s the way it fragmented and diminished at the same time. But those guys told us that in the 50s and 60s they were working nine, ten hours a day. They went from a 50- piece orchestra gig to a live radio show, played a live TV show at night. They were working like crazy. So we caught the tail end of a really fantastic era of recording that was — I feel privileged to have been a part of it.
